title: Familiarity is liking
text: Why do we come to like things simply by seeing them again and again? The mere exposure effect is one of psychology's most {{1}} findings: repeated contact with almost anything — a face, a melody, a nonsense word, even a shape — {{2}} our liking of it. In the founding experiment of 1968, researchers showed volunteers meaningless symbols for a {{3}} of two seconds; the symbols people had seen more often were reliably rated as better. The effect {{4}} music charts and radio playlists: it is why a song grows on us by the fifth play and why advertisers {{5}} the same jingle into every advertising break. It shapes faces too — we prefer the mirror image of our own face, while our friends prefer the true one, because each is the {{6}} they have seen most. There are limits and {{7}}: the effect weakens when the first encounter was bad, and endless repetition can {{8}} boredom as easily as affection. But the deep pattern holds across cultures: to a first approximation, we like what we know — which may explain why the safest strategy for a nervous newcomer is simply to keep turning up.

gaps.explanation: 'one of psychology's most robust findings' — solid and repeatable; rotund = plump, rugged = rough.
'repeated contact increases our liking' — raises it; incite = stir up trouble, incur = bring a cost upon oneself.

gaps.hint: a tiny part (a ___ of two seconds)
gaps.explanation: 'for a fraction of two seconds' — a small part of the time; fracture = a break, friction = rubbing or conflict.
'the effect drives music charts' — powers them; drape = hang loosely, dredge = clear out or dig up.

gaps.hint: push (into every gap), like a pump
gaps.explanation: 'pump the same jingle into every break' — push it in relentlessly; plumb = measure depth or fit pipes.
'each is the image they have seen most' — the visual representation; mirage = an illusion in the desert, imago = an insect's final stage.
'limits and exceptions' — cases where the rule fails; excursion = a short trip, exertion = physical effort.
'repetition can breed boredom' — give rise to it, as in 'familiarity breeds contempt'; braid = plait hair.
